items.title: Agent Distraction
items.summary: Analysis of over 913,000 coding agent sessions reveals that 13% expose agents to inline TODO(b/...) comments. These detours result in significant overhead—adding 70% more steps, 77% more tokens, and 105% more wait time per session—split between chasing closed tickets (41%) and unauthorized scope creep on open bugs (57%). Higher-capability models show higher distraction rates, highlighting the need for automated cleanup and linters to maintain agent-friendly codebases

items.summary: Short answer: use a private object and issue a short-lived presigned URL only after your application has authenticated the customer and authorized the export. The link is a delivery credential, not a replacement for your customer session. Keep the storage object private, pass the bucket, object key, and expiration duration to your storage API, then return the resulting URL to the browser without sending your storage service credentials along with it. That decision matters more than which storage brand you pick. A public object URL is easy to wire and hard to take back. A presigned URL keeps export delivery simple while putting a time limit on the capability. For a small developer-tools product, that is usually the right default: one authorization check in the application, one temporary handoff to the client, and no permanent public access to customer reports. The download endpoint has two separate jobs. First, it must prove that the logged-in customer may read export exp_8f2c. Second, it must obtain a URL that the browser can use to fetch the private object. Mixing those jobs is where many implementations leak access. items.title: Keeping a synthetic voice in sync with a YouTube video: seeks, speed caps and ducking
items.summary: We build DubbingMate, a tool that reads a YouTube video's captions out loud in another language. Getting the words right turned out to be the easy part. Keeping a synthetic voice in step with a video that the viewer pauses, seeks and speeds up was most of the work. Here is what our sync code does today, with the numbers we ended up using. The panel on the right: dubbing is on, the original audio is ducked to 20%, the dub plays at 100%. Every caption cue has a start and an end time. That is the only clock we trust. Before playback we clean the cue list: if a cue ends after the next one starts, we cut its end to the next start, so two lines never compete for the same second. If a video has no captions at all, there is nothing to dub. We do not run our own speech recognition, and the app says so instead of guessing. A sentence that takes 2.1 seconds in English can take 3 seconds in Japanese. items.title: Container Queries and Focus Management: Building Resilient Components with TailwindCSS v4

items.summary: I work on OnePassApps, and we build the browser apps behind this post. This one is the QR Code Maker: it renders a static QR code in your tab and hands back a PNG or an SVG you can print. Every code maker gives you an error-correction level, and almost none of them tell you what that choice does to the file. The panel states its scope up front: "Make a static QR code for a link, text, Wi-Fi, contact, email, phone or SMS, then download it as PNG or SVG." The field hint is "Starts with http or https. https:// is added if you leave it out." and the recovery figure is printed per level: "Level L can recover about 7% of a damaged code. items.title: Integrating Error Tracking for Checkout Reconstruction: 3 Library Practices
items.summary: Short answer: integrate error tracking into the checkout workflow as an evidence pipeline, not as a catch-all exception hook. Capture a stable operation ID, a trace ID, the customer-support-safe request context, and the failure's original cause at each boundary. Then test the event shape with replayable cases before shipping it. That decision is driven by incident reconstruction. A support agent needs to answer which checkout step failed, what the customer saw, and whether a retry changed the outcome. A stack trace alone rarely answers all three. In a Python eval harness, I treat the event schema as an output contract: given the same synthetic checkout failure, the useful fields should be present, redacted, and linked in the same way every time. The simple approach is attractive. Add one global error handler, send the exception, and inspect the dashboard later. It catches an uncaught error, but it loses the timeline around a failure. A payment timeout can look identical to a stale cart or a failed confirmation callback if the event contains only a message and stack. A password-reset message and a generated support report have different risk profiles, even when they leave through the same email pipeline. For the reset flow, keep the template and recipient-data boundary in the application. Let an email service handle transport, suppression, and delivery telemetry. For a report attachment, provider-owned rendering is acceptable only when the support team can change the layout without a deploy and the report contains no unnecessary personal data. That is the useful answer to the selection question. Template ownership is not a compliance certification. It decides who can change wording, who can inspect data during rendering, and what remains recoverable when a message is disputed. Adding a spoken version of your posts does three things: Accessibility – Users with visual impairments or reading difficulties can consume the content. Engagement – Audio keeps visitors on the page longer and can improve SEO signals. Brand personality – A custom voice gives your blog a distinct sound that readers will recognize. All of this is now possible with a few lines of code and a modern text‑to‑speech (TTS) API. There are many options: Google Cloud TTS, Amazon Polly, Azure Speech, and a handful of startups that focus on natural‑sounding voices. For most developers, the sweet spot is a service that: Offers high‑quality, neural voices that sound human. Provides voice cloning so you can use a consistent brand voice. items.title: Our send log counted every email twice because of "Z" vs. "+00:00"
items.summary: I build Galactic Outreach, a tool that finds local businesses and sends them a small, capped number of cold emails. This post is about a bug where a timestamp written two ways made every campaign think it had sent twice as much as it had. It also stopped every campaign at half its daily volume. The dashboard reads Postgres. The mailer, a Node script that does the actual sending, reads plain files: a CSV queue, a CSV send log and a do-not-contact list. That split is deliberate. The mailer is simple, runs from a CLI, and is easy to test against a temp directory. But it means every campaign exists twice, and the two copies have to agree. Before every run, a step called hydration rebuilds the mailer's files from Postgres: The queue and the batch are overwritten, even when the database copy is empty. If a lead was erased in the dashboard, a stale file must not still email them. The send log and the do-not-contact list are merged. Both only ever grow, so the union of the two copies can never lose a contact. That's the safe choice, and it's where the bug was. items.title: Six React chart libraries against hand-written SVG: what I found
items.summary: I worked on an analytics product with about sixteen charts: survival curves, forest plots, histograms and scatter plots. Our charting library had not published a release in over a year. Nothing was broken, but I was worried about future React upgrades and who would maintain it. I wanted to know what we could move to. I took two charts from the product, a survival curve and a scatter plot, and built each with nivo, Recharts, ECharts, visx, TanStack Charts and Chart.js. I also built them in React with hand-written SVG. All seven implementations followed the same spec and used the same synthetic data, with animation off. At typical sizes (three survival series with 200 points each, and a 500-point scatter) the native-speed timings gave me no clear winner. Within each chart type, all seven were less than one frame apart. At 10,000 scatter points, the median mount times spread out: 24 ms for hand-written SVG, 33 ms for visx, 53 ms for TanStack Charts, 80–86 ms for Chart.js and ECharts, 310 ms for Recharts and 3.2 seconds for nivo's SVG scatter. items.title: React Async States That Keep Forms Honest
items.summary: Forms are where a polished product can suddenly feel unreliable. A user submits an email, the button spins, and then… nothing useful happens. Maybe the request is still running. Maybe the server rejected the address. Maybe the response succeeded but the UI forgot to move on. In React, this often starts with a harmless-looking isLoading boolean. Over time it becomes a bucket for validation, network work, success messages, retries, and failures. The component still works, but it is hard to explain and harder to recover. The better approach is to give the form a small, explicit async state model. It makes the JavaScript easier to reason about, and it gives users a clearer product experience. Consider this common shape: const [isLoading, setIsLoading] = useState(false); const [error, setError] = useState(null); It looks simple until you ask a few questions: Should a second submit be blocked while client validation runs? Can the user edit the field after a server error? Does an old response still have permission to overwrite a newer attempt? What should the button say after success? items.summary: Exploiting a JWT implementation that uses a weak signing secret to crack the key, forge admin credentials, and access restricted endpoints. The OopsSec Store signs its JWTs with a weak secret. We'll crack it, forge an admin token, and walk right into the restricted dashboard. Spin up the OopsSec Store in a new directory: npx create-oss-store oss-store cd oss-store npm start Or with Docker (no Node.js required): docker run -p 127.0.0.1:3000:3000 leogra/oss-oopssec-store Head to http://localhost:3000 and log in with the test credentials shown on the login page. Use Alice's account -- she's a regular customer. The app uses JWTs for session management. After login, the server drops a token in an HTTP-only cookie that tags along with every request. There's a link to /admin sitting right there in the footer. Click it as Alice and you get an access denied page. Open DevTools, go to Application > Cookies. The token is in an HTTP-only cookie called authToken. Paste it into jwt.io: Header: { "alg": "HS256", "typ": "JWT" } Payload: { "id": "cmk7hzehr0001togvwvjt810d", "email": "alice@example.com", "role": "CUSTOMER", "hint": "The secret is not so secret", "exp": 1768763557 } HS256 -- HMAC-SHA

When I rewrote the backend as a separate Web API, I didn't bring Hangfire with me. The API that serves this page runs two BackgroundService classes fed by System.Threading.Channels, and one WHERE clause does the work of the every-minute job. This isn't a "Hangfire is bad" post. Hangfire is a good library. It's a post about checking which jobs actually needed it, because for this site the answer was none of them. The short version: Use Hangfire (or Quartz.NET) when a job must survive a restart, retry on its own, or be visible on a dashboard. If the work is in-process, short-lived and fine to lose on a crash, a BackgroundService with a bounded Channel is built into .NET, needs no extra database, and is about 60 lines. A job that only "flips something on at a certain time" often needs no job at all: filter by time in the query. items.title: Prevent Spoofed Orders in Next.js Telegram Mini Apps using Server-Validated MainButton Checkout
items.summary: Shipping an e-commerce storefront inside a Telegram Mini App using Next.js App Router seems straightforward until untrusted client state compromises your checkout process. Front-end developers frequently rely on window.Telegram.WebApp.initDataUnsafe to identify the user and send cart totals directly from the client to an API route. Because initDataUnsafe can be mutated by anyone opening your app in a standard browser or using browser developer tools, accepting unverified user IDs or total prices from the front end allows users to modify invoice amounts, impersonate other customer accounts, or execute unverified orders. Building a robust Telegram Mini App shop requires verifying the raw initData payload using an HMAC-SHA256 signature on the server, calculating cart prices strictly from stored backend database values, controlling Telegram's native MainButton across React render lifecycles, and accounting for renderer discrepancies between iOS WebViews and Telegram Desktop. items.title: Britain to Make Salary Disclosure In Job Ads Mandatory
items.summary: Britain plans to require employers to disclose salaries in job advertisements. "Whether you're a young person starting out or a parent trying to support your family, you should know what a job pays before spending your time and effort applying for it," Prime Minister Andy Burnham said in a statement. Reuters reports: The government said requiring companies to disclose pay in job ads would help young people applying for their first jobs, while boosting pay transparency and helping tackle disparities that can disadvantage women. Just over two in five employers always publish salary ranges, while fewer than one in five always disclose specific salaries, Burnham's office said, citing estimates from the Chartered Institute of Personnel and Development. The government will soon introduce legislation to parliament making salary disclosures mandatory, Burnham's office said, although it did not provide a timeline. Nearly one million, or 13%, of 16 to 24 year-olds in Britain are not in employment, education or training, one of the highest shares in Europe. A government review into youth inactivity is due to be published later in November. Read more of this story at Slashdot.

items.title: When “Working as Designed” Is the Problem
items.summary: I submitted a security report to Anthropic after Claude Code exposed my .NET User Secrets in its model context. They classified it as “Informative – Working as Designed.” “Working as designed” is a triage label, not a verdict. But taken at face value, it points to something architectural: security is enforced tool by tool, not around the agent as a whole, and certainly not at the OS-boundary level. .NET developers commonly use dotnet user-secrets to keep development credentials in their user profile, outside the project tree. These secrets can include: • API keys • Database connection strings • Passwords • Third-party service credentials • Other sensitive application configuration Consider this scenario: You have a .NET application. You have configured User Secrets. You launch Claude Code in your project directory. You ask Claude to inspect your application configuration. Claude can execute: dotnet user-secrets list And/or read the plaintext secrets.json file. %APPDATA%\Microsoft\UserSecrets\ \secrets.json Because tool output is returned to Claude, those credentials become part of the conversation context. items.title: Permission-heavy multi-tenant systems: make the access check boring
items.summary: Permission-heavy systems become risky when access rules are scattered across controllers, UI checks, repository filters, and background jobs. The aim is not a clever authorization framework. It is one rule path that is difficult to bypass. The examples come from Shield, Zotic, CAS, Question Banking and Amlaak. Every protected operation can be described with four values: the actor, the tenant, the action, and the resource. If one is unknown, the system does not yet have enough information to allow the operation. This simple tuple prevents a common mistake: checking that a user has a permission somewhere, then loading a resource that belongs to another tenant. Permission and ownership need to be evaluated together. The decision input public sealed record AccessRequest( Guid ActorId, Guid TenantId, string Action, string ResourceType, Guid? ResourceId); A route parameter or request body can name a tenant, but it cannot prove membership in that tenant. Resolve the active tenant from authenticated membership, then compare any requested tenant identifier with it. items.title: Building a service status notifier with .NET and Cloudflare Workers
items.summary: I've been working on a small side project recently. Like most developers I depend on quite a few external services. GitHub, Cloudflare, OpenAI, and others. When something breaks, I usually end up checking their individual status pages to figure out what's going on. I wanted a simpler way to keep track of these incidents and get notified in Slack without having to configure every provider separately. So I started building StatusRelay. Why build another status monitoring tool? Of course, tools like this already exist, and they offer much more comprehensive solutions. I wasn't trying to reinvent everything they do. I just wanted something lightweight where I could select the services I care about, connect a Slack channel or webhook, and start receiving notifications. No accounts, no paid plans, and no complicated setup. It also seemed like a fun opportunity to experiment with event processing, background jobs, and reliable notification delivery. But how does it work?! The idea is pretty straightforward: Poll official status APIs from different providers. Normalize their status and incident information. Store incidents and detect changes. Send notifications to Slack or custom webhooks.

items.title: Building MCP Servers in .NET for AI Agents, a 10-part tutorial series
items.summary: If you're a .NET developer and you want to build an MCP server, it's hard to know where to start. Most examples stop at a "hello world" tool running on your own machine. I wanted a series that goes from that first tool all the way to a server that real users can sign in to and use from different AI clients. So I wrote one. items.title: I Stamped Every Row With DateTime.Now and Paid Twice
items.summary: I had a batch importer stamping DateTime.Now onto every row it processed. A few hundred thousand rows, one timestamp each, nothing I'd ever think twice about. Then I put a profiler on the thing because it was slower than it had any right to be, and there it was near the top: reading the clock. Not the database, not the parsing. The clock. So I did the thing I always end up doing. I counted. DateTime.Now doesn't read a "local clock." There's no such thing. It reads UTC, exactly like DateTime.UtcNow does, and then converts that instant into local time using TimeZoneInfo.Local. That conversion is the whole difference between the two calls. One reads the clock. The other reads the clock and then asks the time zone database what your offset is right now, DST and all. The offset lookup is the part that costs. And here's the bit that surprised me: it costs even when the answer is zero. I read each one 20 million times, summed the ticks so nothing got optimized away, best of five rounds. items.title: They Created a Cell That's Almost Alive. What to Do With It Now? (8 minute read)
items.summary: A SpudCell is an artificial cell created from lifeless ingredients that can grow, copy its DNA, divide in two, and start its cell cycle all over again. It is still far from a self-sustaining cell that any scientist could manufacture from prepared ingredients, but the technology could eventually make it easier to produce medicines, foods, and other items that could not otherwise be produced with ordinary biology. The researchers working on SpudCell hope that it will eventually be a platform for biotechnology that will allow a simple cell to be engineered in scores of useful ways. SpudCell could potentially be misused, so its researchers are taking security seriously from the start - its DNA and proteins are engineered so that it can only survive on an exotic diet of chemicals not found in nature.

items.title: OpenAI Responds to US Midterm Elections With New Commitment to Communities
items.summary: "OpenAI has published a new National Community Compact and Compute Campus Policy Blueprint, apparently in response to the Blue Wave Midterm Elections," writes ancient Slashdot reader Gilmoure. "Instead of moving into communities like a juggernaut, they say they will be dangling friendly carrots going forward." Here's an excerpt from OpenAI's article: Every future compute campus OpenAI owns and operates will have its own local compact. We'll engage residents early enough to ensure their input shapes project plans, give them a local point of contact throughout the life of the campus, and report publicly each year on how we're doing. Each compact will reflect local priorities and include a common set of commitments: - Pay our own way on energy and infrastructure. We'll pay the full cost of the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve us. Before major spending begins, we'll provide financial assurances so other customers are protected if a project is delayed, reduced, or canceled. - Protect local resources and report on our impact. We'll develop a water plan for each campus, prioritize closed-loop or low-water cooling, and publish site-level water and electricity use.

items.title: OpenSSH Flaw Lets Attackers Log Into Password-Disabled Linux Accounts
items.summary: A newly disclosed OpenSSH flaw dubbed "*sshole" can allow attackers to log in to password-disabled accounts on certain musl-based Linux systems simply by submitting a password longer than 256 bytes. "Apparently certain varieties of musl Linux (Alpine, OpenWrt, Buildroot, Yocto, etc.) have had this OpenSSH vulnerability for about a decade," writes longtime Slashdot reader AlteredEgg. "Upgrade now!" BleepingComputer reports: Security researcher Ozgun Kultekin, who discovered and released details on the vulnerability today, says the flaw has existed since 2016 and stems from how OpenSSH handles password verification errors on systems using the musl C library. Linux accounts can be configured to prevent password logins by replacing their password hash with an asterisk (*) in the /etc/shadow file. Because this is not a valid password hash, no password should allow access to those accounts. However, a patch introduced in OpenSSH in 2016 to fix a username enumeration vulnerability tracked as CVE-2016-6210 changed how OpenSSH handled accounts without usable password hashes. items.summary: When we started building Brass Pawn (source on GitHub, AGPLv3), we needed a large offline tactics, positional judgement, and endgame dataset that ran completely on-device—both in the browser and natively on iPhone, iPad, and Mac. Transcribing chess puzzles by hand or scraping unverified problem collections breaks down fast. Two failure modes show up immediately in real training: Cooked solutions: A position has a flashy sacrifice, so a human annotator marks it as winning—missing a quiet defensive resource at depth 18, or missing a second equally winning move that punishes a student for playing an objectively strong alternative. Horizon flips: A shallow engine pass (depth 10–12) flags a move as +2.10, only for depth 22 to reveal perpetual check (0.00). Instead of transcribing puzzles, we built a deterministic mining and independent verification pipeline powered by Stockfish 18. Along the way, we hit a subtle FEN validation edge case in chess.js that silently breaks UCI engines. A good tactics puzzle isn't simply "someone blundered in a game." items.title: Making a SwiftUI app survive a folding iPhone: what broke on the iPhone Duo and how I fixed it
items.summary: I make PawLife, a small pet health app (feeding plans in grams, a health diary, a food safety lookup). It is one SwiftUI codebase for iPhone, iPad, Mac Catalyst, Apple Watch and visionOS. When Xcode 27.2 shipped simulators for the iPhone Duo, I expected "it is just a wider iPhone". It is not. Here is what actually broke, in the order I found it, and what the fixes looked like. The Duo has an outer display and an inner one across the fold. Your app runs on one of them at a time, and the window changes size when the user folds or unfolds. The simulator reports it as a window resize, not a new scene. Measured on the simulator: Folded: a 466×678 pt window, of which my app got 382 pt of width. The remaining 84 pt on the trailing edge is a reserved column (status area and camera) exposed through the safe area. Open: a landscape 951×669 pt window, 867 pt for the app, with the same 84 pt trailing column. So the app goes from a narrow portrait phone to a wide landscape slab and back, live, without a relaunch. items.title: iOS silent push not working: content-available and background pushes
items.summary: A silent push, which Apple calls a background notification, has no alert, sound or badge. It wakes your app so it can fetch new content. Apple treats it as low priority and does not guarantee delivery, so "it worked once and then stopped" is often the system working as designed. This page goes through what must be right on the sender and in the app, and what the device itself decides. What you see Likely cause Fix Never arrives, alert pushes work Remote notifications background mode not ticked Signing and Capabilities > Background Modes > Remote notification Shows a banner instead of waking the app quietly alert, sound or badge in aps next to content-available Send aps with content-available: 1 and nothing else APNs returns 400 apns-priority: 10 with apns-push-type: background Priority 5 for background pushes, always Delivered late, or in bursts Priority 5 pushes are sent according to the device's power state Expected; use an alert push for anything a person waits for Arrives in testing, then stops Throttled: too many background pushes Two or three an hour at most Nothing after the user swiped the app away The app was force quit Nothing to fix; it wakes again once the user opens it

items.title: Understanding SwiftUI's layoutPriority: HStack, ZStack, and Custom Layouts
items.summary: SwiftUI makes building interfaces straightforward, but its layout system can sometimes produce unexpected results. One modifier that developers often reach for is .layoutPriority(). For example: swift This can help resolve layout issues, but what exactly does the priority value mean? And does the modifier behave the same way in every container? To explore these questions, I built an interactive open-source project called SwiftUI Layout Lab. The .layoutPriority() modifier provides a priority value that parent layouts can use when determining how to size their children. The default priority is 0. A higher priority doesn't directly specify a width, height, or percentage of available space. Its effect depends on the parent layout algorithm and the sizing behavior of the child views. For example, assigning a priority of 100 doesn't mean a view will receive 100 times more space than a view with priority 1. An HStack arranges views horizontally, but what happens when there isn't enough space for every view to receive its preferred width? In Layout Lab, you can: Select one of three views. Change its layout priority. Adjust the available container width. Observe the actual measured widths.

items.title: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. Coding agents in a native Mac app
items.summary: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. I built Coincide as a native Mac app for the coding agents I already use. Here is a new 10-second motion preview: A Mac interface built with Swift and AppKit Coincide's main interface is built with AppKit, with SwiftUI where it fits, such as Settings. It brings native menus, Mac keyboard shortcuts, a native transcript and the agent/model picker into one window. The clip calls out the architecture: Swift. AppKit. No Electron. That describes Coincide's Mac interface. It isn't a benchmark or a claim that every workload is faster than another app. Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Grok Build, OpenCode and Antigravity each run through their own command-line tool and existing login. Coincide does not sell or meter tokens. When you switch agents mid-thread, the next agent gets a recap of the turns it missed and works in the same directory. Each agent keeps its own native session. Switching back resumes that agent's session. The handoff deep dive covers the mechanism and its limits. The preview browses Codex, Claude Code and Cursor's picker catalogs. Available models depend on the agents installed and the provider account you use. This is an edited illustrative demo:

items.title: Crop Once, Post Everywhere: Batch Aspect-Ratio Crops for Social Images in Swift
items.summary: If you ship photos from an iPhone app to more than one place, you eventually hit the same boring problem: Instagram wants 1:1 or 4:5, a shop banner wants 16:9, Stories want 9:16, and the camera roll is full of 4:3 and 3:4 stills. Doing that crop by hand for thirty product shots is how afternoons disappear. This post walks through a small UIKit pipeline that takes one UIImage, a list of target aspect ratios, and returns one centre-weighted crop per ratio — suitable for running across a whole album. I’m writing it from the seat of someone who builds BatchMark, an on-device batch photo app, where “apply the same finishing step to many photos” is the whole product. The code below is a teaching extract, not a dump of the app. People say “crop to 1:1” and mean two different things: Aspect-fill crop: keep the photo’s resolution as high as possible, cut off the edges that don’t fit the ratio. Aspect-fit pad: show the whole photo, add bars (or a mat) to reach the ratio. For social uploads you almost always want (1). items.title: Wireway – a native macOS HTTPS proxy with a built-in MCP server

items.title: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time review – a dream come true
items.summary: Nintendo Switch 2; Nintendo This ambitious remake transforms a landmark Zelda game into a modern masterpiece, clearer and easier to navigate, more beautiful to look at, with playful musical touches. Yet the melancholy remains It’s always a worry, returning to a formative piece of art from your childhood. Will your jaded adult sensibilities render you unable to locate the magic that captivated your child self? Will revisiting it reveal that it was never actually that good, and that your tastes are built on a foundation of lies? With video games, there is the added complication of technological advancement: decades-old games can look so basic and feel so treacly to play that it’s hard to explain why they were mind-blowing at the time. Light-touch remasters aim to bring such games up to modern graphical standards without fundamentally changing them; an ambitious remake attempts to transform the work into something that can stand alongside any modern masterpiece. Ocarina of Time is the latter. And I could not be more delighted to report that it is a dream come true. Continue reading...

items.summary: An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. items.title: I’m a CTO. AI still needs your human expertise | Madhu Shashanka
items.summary: AI is increasingly getting good at doing some tasks, but it can never replace human workers’ judgment Autonomous cars, which may be the safest we have built, keep getting easily avoidable parking tickets. While Waymos crash far less often than human drivers over tens of millions of miles, they’re still terrible at performing basic tasks – keeping out of disabled parking spots and tow-away zones, or steering clear of a church garage during Sunday service, according to the Wall Street Journal. That is the state of AI today: impressively capable at something complex, yet embarrassingly clumsy at something easy. And it has implications for what work will remain human and what will be automated by AI. Madhu Shashanka is co-founder, chief scientist and chief technology officer at Concentric AI, a data security software company Continue reading...
